title: Jump k Steps Up the Tree

concept.title: Binary lifting: store the 1st, 2nd, 4th, 8th, ... ancestor of every node
body: The *k-th ancestor* of a node is the node reached by going up `k` times along the parents (the 0th ancestor is the node itself; the parent of the root does not exist). Going up one step at a time costs O(k) per query, which is O(n) on a long path, and too slow for 20000 queries on 20000 nodes.

*Binary lifting* uses the binary representation of `k`. Precompute a table `up[j][v]`: the **2^j-th ancestor** of `v` (or 0 if there is none). The first row is the parent, and each next row is made from the previous one: going up `2^j` steps is going up `2^(j-1)` steps twice.

Use 0 as the "no node" value, with `up[j][0] = 0`, so that jumping beyond the root keeps the result 0 (print -1 then). A `k` of at least `n` is always beyond the root. The table has `LOG * n` entries and is built in O(n log n); every query takes O(log n). The same table solves the lowest common ancestor problem, in the next task.

statement: A tree with `n` nodes is given by the parent of each node (0 for the root). For each query `v k`, print the k-th ancestor of the node `v` (the node reached by going up `k` times; for `k = 0` it is `v` itself), or -1 if the road upward ends before `k` steps.
inputFormat: The first line has `n`, the number of nodes (numbered 1 to n).
The second line has `n` numbers: for each node its parent, and 0 for the root.
The third line has `q`, the number of queries.
Each of the next `q` lines has a node `v` and a number `k`.
constraints: The numbers describe one tree: exactly one node has the parent 0, and following parents always reaches it.
A parent can have a larger number than its child.
The tree can be a long path (depth up to n - 1).

examples.note: Node 4 has the parent 2, whose parent is 1, the root: 2, 1, -1; and node 7 is its own 0th ancestor: 7.

hints: Make a table up[j][v] with the 2^j-th ancestor of every node; each row comes from the previous row.
Use 0 as "no node" and keep it at 0 in every row.
For a query go through the bits of k and jump up[j][v] for every bit that is set; answer -1 if you end at 0.

explanation: The table up[j][v] holds the 2^j-th ancestor of v (0 if none), each row built from the previous one. A query jumps once for every set bit of k; ending at 0 (or k >= n) means there is no such ancestor.
solution.complexity: Time O(n log n + q log n), space O(n log n).
